segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Truly, truly, I tell you, whoever does not enter the sheepfold through the gate but climbs in some other way—that one is a thief and a bandit.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: But the one who enters through the gate is the shepherd of the sheep.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: The gatekeeper opens for him, and the sheep listen to his voice. He calls his own sheep by name and leads them out.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: When he has brought out all his own, he goes ahead of them, and the sheep follow him, because they know his voice.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: A stranger they will never follow; they will run away from him, because they do not know the voice of strangers.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jesus told them this figure of speech, but they did not understand what it was that he was saying to them.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So Jesus said to them again,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Truly, truly, I tell you, I am the gate for the sheep.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: All who came before me are thieves and bandits, but the sheep did not listen to them.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: I am the gate. Whoever enters through me will be saved, and will come in and go out and find pasture.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: The thief comes only to steal and slaughter and destroy. I came so that they may have life, and have it in abundance.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: The hired hand, who is not a shepherd and does not own the sheep, sees the wolf coming, leaves the sheep, and runs away, and the wolf snatches them and scatters them.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: He runs away because he is a hired hand and does not care about the sheep.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: I am the good shepherd. I know my own and my own know me,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: just as the Father knows me and I know the Father; and I lay down my life for the sheep.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: I have other sheep too, which are not of this fold. I must bring them also, and they will listen to my voice, and there will be one flock, one shepherd.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: This is why the Father loves me: I lay down my life so that I may take it up again.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: No one takes it from me; I lay it down of my own accord. I have authority to lay it down, and I have authority to take it up again. This command I received from my Father.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Again there was a division among the Jews because of these words.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Many of them were saying,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “He has a demon and is out of his mind! Why listen to him?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Others were saying,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “These are not the words of someone possessed by a demon. Can a demon open the eyes of the blind?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then came the Festival of Dedication in Jerusalem. It was winter,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and Jesus was walking in the temple, in Solomon’s Colonnade.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So the Jews surrounded him and said to him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “How long will you keep us in suspense? If you are the Messiah, tell us plainly.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jesus answered them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “I told you, and you do not believe. The works that I do in my Father’s name—these testify about me;

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: but you do not believe, because you do not belong to my sheep.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: My sheep listen to my voice; I know them, and they follow me.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: I give them eternal life, and they will never perish, and no one will snatch them out of my hand.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: As for what my Father has given me, he is greater than all, and no one can snatch it out of the Father’s hand.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: I and the Father are one.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Again the Jews picked up stones to stone him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jesus answered them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “I have shown you many good works from the Father. For which of these works are you stoning me?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The Jews answered him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “We are not stoning you for a good work but for blasphemy, because you, a human being, make yourself God.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jesus answered them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Is it not written in your Law, ‘I said, you are gods’?

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: If he called them ‘gods’ to whom the word of God came, and the Scripture cannot be broken,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: do you say to the one whom the Father consecrated and sent into the world, ‘You are blaspheming,’ because I said, ‘I am God’s Son’?

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: If I am not doing the works of my Father, do not believe me.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: But if I am doing them, then even if you do not believe me, believe the works, so that you may come to know and keep on knowing that the Father is in me and I am in the Father.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So they were again trying to seize him, but he escaped from their hands.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He went away again across the Jordan to the place where John had first been baptizing, and he stayed there.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Many came to him and were saying,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “John performed no sign, but everything John said about this man was true.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And many believed in him there.

notes.note: Greek distinguishes the thief, who steals by stealth, from this word, which names an armed and violent plunderer such as a highwayman or brigand. “Robber” is the usual rendering and is not wrong, but in modern English it can suggest a burglar; “bandit” keeps the violence and outlawry. Standard lexicons give robber, highwayman or bandit, and note that the word was also applied to insurrectionists.

The Greek word covers any entrance that opens and shuts. The older English tradition has “door,” as in “I am the door” (verses 7 and 9); because the picture here is the entrance to a walled sheep enclosure, “gate” is the natural English word, and several modern translations use it. The meaning is not in dispute.

John does not use the word for “parable” found in the other Gospels. His word means a proverb or a veiled, figurative saying, and he later contrasts it with speaking “plainly” (16:25, 29). Older versions have “parable” here; most modern ones have “figure of speech.”

John often uses this term for a particular group in Jerusalem that disputes with Jesus, not for the Jewish people as a whole; Jesus, his disciples and those who defend him in verse 21 are also Jews. Here and in verses 24–33 the group is not clearly identified as the authorities, so the general term is kept. Some scholars prefer “Judeans” or “the Jewish leaders” in such passages.

This is the festival now known as Hanukkah. It commemorates the rededication of the Jerusalem temple in 164 BC, after its desecration under the Seleucid king Antiochus IV. It lasts eight days and falls in December, hence “it was winter.”

notes.traditional: make us to doubt; keep us in suspense
notes.note: The Greek idiom is literally “How long are you lifting up our life?” Nearly all modern translations understand it as holding someone in suspense. Evidence for the idiom outside this verse is thin, and some interpreters take it instead as “How long will you annoy us?”

The Greek word translates the Hebrew title for the anointed king Israel expected. Here the questioners are asking about that title, not using a name, so “Messiah” conveys what they meant. Several modern translations use “Messiah” in such places in the Gospels and keep “Christ” where it functions as a name.

notes.phrase: As for what my Father has given me, he is greater than all
notes.traditional: My Father, who has given them to me, is greater than all
notes.note: The manuscripts differ here in two small words, giving either “My Father, who has given them to me, is greater than all” (the reading most English versions follow) or “What my Father has given me is greater than all.” The Greek text followed here combines a neuter “what” with a masculine “greater,” which is grammatically rough. The rendering keeps both: “what my Father has given me” is set out in front as the topic, and “greater” is taken as describing the Father. The Greek gives no object for “snatch”; the “it” is supplied and refers back to what the Father has given.

The Greek word for “one” is neuter: “one thing,” not “one person.” In context the claim concerns unity in keeping the sheep, since no one can snatch them from either hand, and the hearers take it as a claim to divine status (verse 33). How far the statement reaches beyond unity of action and purpose toward unity of being has been debated since antiquity.

The Greek has no article, so the phrase can be read “make yourself God” or “make yourself a god.” Most translations choose “God,” which fits the charge of blasphemy. Jesus’s reply in verses 34–36 turns on the plural “gods,” which suggests the looser sense is also in view.

The quotation is from Psalm 82:6, so “Law” here stands for the Scriptures as a whole, not only the books of Moses. In the psalm God addresses a group as “gods”; ancient and modern interpreters have identified them variously as Israel’s judges, members of a heavenly council, or Israel receiving the Law at Sinai. The argument runs from the lesser to the greater: if Scripture can use the word of them, it is not blasphemy for the one the Father sent to call himself God’s Son.

The verb is built on the ordinary word for “holy” and means to bring someone or something into the sphere of what belongs to God. Here the point is that the Father set Jesus apart for a mission, not that he changed his moral state, so “consecrated” is used in place of the traditional “sanctified.” Several modern translations render it “consecrated” or “set apart” in this verse; the meaning is not disputed.

notes.phrase: come to know and keep on knowing
notes.note: The Greek uses the same verb twice in two different forms, the first pointing to the moment of coming to know and the second to knowing as a continuing state. Most translations vary the English (“know and understand”); this rendering keeps the repetition. Some manuscripts replace the second verb with “believe.”

warnings: Verse 36: βλασφημέω is not rendered with a register form (slander; blaspheme; insult / hurl insults at / hurl insults) and has no register-exception note.

findings.greek: ὁ πατήρ μου ὃ δέδωκέν μοι πάντων μεῖζων ἐστίν
findings.english: My Father, who has given them to me, is greater than all
findings.problem: The relative pronoun ὃ is neuter ('what/that which'), not masculine ὅς ('who'). The Greek says that what the Father has given to Jesus is greater than all. The English makes the Father the subject of 'is greater' and supplies 'them', which follows a different reading.

findings.greek: ὁ πατήρ μου ὃ δέδωκέν μοι πάντων μεῖζων ἐστίν
findings.english: As for what my Father has given me, he is greater than all
findings.problem: In the SBLGNT reading, the neuter relative ὃ (what the Father has given) is the subject of 'is greater than all'. The English makes the Father ('he') the one who is greater, which follows the variant reading ὃς instead.

changed.before: My Father, who has given them to me, is greater than all, and no one can snatch them out of the Father’s hand.
changed.after: As for what my Father has given me, he is greater than all, and no one can snatch it out of the Father’s hand.
